Best exercises for rheumatoid arthritis in hands and wrists — RA most commonly begins in the small joints of the hands and wrists. Regular hand and wrist exercises are one of the most important self-management strategies for maintaining grip strength, reducing stiffness and preserving function.

Quick answer: Best exercises for RA hands and wrists: tendon gliding, wrist flexion/extension, radial/ulnar deviation, soft foam grip squeezes, finger spreading. Do after morning stiffness eases, soak hands in warm water first. During flares: range-of-motion only, no resistance. Expect reduced stiffness in 2-3 weeks.

Why Hand Exercises Are Essential in RA

RA causes synovitis (inflammation of the joint lining) in the hand and wrist joints, leading to pain, swelling and — if untreated — joint damage and deformity. Exercise does not cure or stop the inflammatory process, but it maintains the strength and range of motion that functional deformity threatens to reduce. NICE guidance recommends hand exercises as part of standard RA management.

The Core Hand and Wrist Programme

Tendon Gliding Exercises

Start with hand flat (extension), make a hook (straight fingers bent at middle joints), then full fist, then straight fist (fingers bent, thumb alongside). Hold each position 3 seconds. 10 repetitions each hand. These maintain full tendon movement through the hand.

Wrist Flexion and Extension

Rest forearm on a table, hand extending over the edge. Slowly bend wrist downward (flexion) and upward (extension) through full range. 10 repetitions each direction, both wrists.

Radial and Ulnar Deviation

Forearm flat, palm down. Move hand toward thumb side (radial deviation), then little finger side (ulnar deviation). 10 repetitions. Important for maintaining wrist side-to-side movement often lost early in RA wrist disease.

Pinch and Grip Strengthening

Squeeze a soft foam ball or rolled-up towel 10 times each hand. Pinch a clothes peg open using thumb and each finger in turn. Do not use hard grip strengtheners during active inflammation — the resistance is too high.

Finger Spreading

Place hand flat on table. Spread fingers as wide as possible, hold 3 seconds, bring together. 10 repetitions. Maintains MCP joint mobility.

Timing and Flare Management

Perform exercises after morning stiffness has eased — typically 1–2 hours after waking or after medication has taken effect. Warm water soaking (5 minutes in warm water) before exercises significantly reduces stiffness. During a flare: gentle range-of-motion only, no resistance work. Resume strengthening 2–3 days after swelling reduces.

Q&A

Question: Should I wear splints alongside exercises?
Short answer: Resting splints worn at night reduce joint loading and morning stiffness in RA. Working splints (softer, worn during activity) can support wrists during tasks. An occupational therapist can advise on the right type for your specific pattern of involvement.

Question: When will I notice improvement?
Short answer: Reduced morning stiffness is typically noticed within 2–3 weeks of consistent daily practice. Grip strength improvements take 6–8 weeks.

Practical next steps for Best Exercises for Rheumatoid Arthritis in Hands and Wrists

If you came here about Best Exercises for Rheumatoid Arthritis in Hands and Wrists, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your NHS trust about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Pacing on good and bad days

On better days it is tempting to catch up on everything at once. Spread chores and exercise across the week instead. Use the two-hour rule many physiotherapists suggest: if pain or fatigue is clearly worse two hours after activity, the dose was too high — trim the next session rather than stopping altogether.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Peer support etiquette

Share what helps you without prescribing it for others. Conditions, medicines and life circumstances differ. If someone is in crisis, encourage them toward NHS 111, their GP, or emergency services rather than relying on a forum alone.

Quick questions about Best Exercises Rheumatoid Arthritis

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
